c.tagline: Ancient Sahel trading city of mud-walled markets, indigo dye pits, and Hausa heritage.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis and shared drop taxis are unmetered, so agree the fare before setting off. Keke NAPEP tricycles handle most short trips; app-based Bolt and inDrive give fixed upfront prices.

emergency.note: 112 is Nigeria's national emergency number; response times can be slow, so private hospitals and clinics are usually the most reliable option for medical care.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: A dense, bustling commercial district near the central business area between the Old City and Sabon Gari, full of markets, trading, and cheap eateries; convenient and lively but noisy and congested.
Kano's leafy Government Reserved Area with wide streets, government buildings, consulates, and most of the city's better hotels and restaurants; the calmest and most upscale base for visitors.

The historic 'strangers' quarter' settled by southern Nigerian and other non-Hausa migrants, home to a large market and most of the city's bars and nightlife (unusual for Kano); diverse and lively, but keep security awareness.
A mixed industrial and residential area northeast of the center with factories, offices, and several mid-range hotels; practical for business travelers but less atmospheric for tourists.

water.note: Tap water isn't reliably treated; drink only bottled or well-filtered water.

transit.hours: Minibuses and shared taxis run roughly from dawn until mid-evening; Keke NAPEP tricycles cover short trips throughout the day, with far fewer options after dark, when app rides or private taxis are safer.
transit.note: Kano has no metro, tram, or urban rail; travel is by shared minibuses, drop (shared) taxis, and ubiquitous Keke NAPEP tricycles, supplemented by Bolt and inDrive ride-hailing.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor; there is no rechargeable transit card system. Carry small naira notes for exact change.

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up or leaving small change for good service is appreciated. Some upscale hotels and restaurants add a service charge.

food.name: Tuwo shinkafa with miyan kuka
food.desc: Soft pounded-rice dumpling served with a dark, tangy soup of powdered baobab leaf and dried fish or beef - the definitive Hausa lunch.

places.name: Ten to Ten Restaurant
places.note: Calm, cosy dining room known for tuwo served with kuka, taushe and aleho soups.

places.name: Kurmi Market food stalls
places.area: Old City, near the Emir's Palace
places.note: Centuries-old market where cooks ladle tuwo and kuka from clay pots at midday.

places.name: Yankaba Market cook shops
places.note: Busy local buka row; the queues at noon tell you which pot is freshest.

food.name: Suya
food.desc: Thin beef or mutton rubbed with yaji - ground peanut, ginger, chili and paprika - and grilled over charcoal, served on newspaper with raw onion and tomato.

places.name: Uba Suya
places.note: Named repeatedly in local guides as the go-to for authentic Kano suya.

places.name: Sabon Gari evening suya stalls
places.note: The classic Kano suya strip; grills fire up after dusk and run late.

places.name: Zoo Road suya grills
places.note: Roadside mai suya stands popular with families and students in the evening.

food.name: Kilishi
food.desc: Beef sliced paper-thin, coated in a spiced groundnut paste and sun-dried into a sweet-hot jerky. Kano's most famous edible souvenir - buy it vacuum-packed.

places.name: Zoo Road kilishi sellers
places.note: Kano's best-known kilishi row; racks of it drying and sold by weight.

places.name: Kurmi Market
places.note: Traditional traders sell kilishi alongside spices and dyed cloth in the old market.

places.name: Sabon Gari Market
places.note: Convenient stalls for packaged kilishi to take home; haggle by the bundle.

food.name: Masa (waina)
food.desc: Small fermented rice cakes fried in a dimpled pan until crisp-edged and fluffy, eaten with pepper sauce, honey or a bowl of miyan taushe.

places.name: Kofar Mata morning masa stalls
places.note: Griddles going from sunrise near the historic dye pits; eaten standing with yaji.

places.name: Sabon Gari street vendors
places.note: Masa and kosai sold hot from roadside pans for breakfast and evening snacks.

places.name: Ten to Ten Restaurant
places.note: Sit-down option if you want masa with a proper bowl of soup rather than on the street.

food.name: Danwake
food.desc: Bean-flour and cassava dumplings boiled, then tossed with groundnut oil, pepper, kuli-kuli crumbs and onion - a cheap, filling Hausa street breakfast.

places.name: Yankaba Market stalls
places.note: Women sell danwake by the bowl each morning; ask for extra kuli-kuli on top.

places.name: Kofar Mata street stalls
places.note: Old-city corner stands serving danwake and alkaki to the market crowd.

places.name: Rimi Market food row
places.note: Reliable spot for the morning bean-dumpling stalls near the trading stalls.

food.name: Balangu
food.desc: Whole cuts of mutton or beef roasted slowly over wood embers, then chopped and salted at the counter - juicier and less spiced than suya.

places.name: Sabon Gari grill row
places.note: Balangu pits alongside the suya stalls; go early evening before the best cuts sell out.

places.name: Kofar Ruwa balangu spots
places.note: Old-city roasters working over wood fires, a favourite of Kano regulars.

places.name: Zoo Road roadside roasters
places.note: Easy to find and busy, which means fast turnover and fresh meat.

food.name: Zobo
food.desc: Deep-red hibiscus infusion steeped with ginger, cloves and pineapple, served ice cold. Kano is a dry, sharia state, and zobo is what everyone drinks instead.

places.name: Kurmi Market drink sellers
places.note: Chilled zobo poured from coolers in the market lanes for a few naira.

places.name: Ado Bayero Mall food court
places.note: Air-conditioned option with bottled zobo and kunu made fresh daily.

places.name: Sabon Gari street vendors
places.note: Bagged and bottled zobo sold beside the evening suya grills.

food.name: Kunun zaki
food.desc: Lightly spiced millet drink, cloudy and gently sweet with ginger and tamarind, drunk cold as a meal-in-a-glass - especially in Ramadan.

places.name: Yankaba Market vendors
places.note: Home-made kunu sold from calabashes and bottles each morning.

places.name: Kurmi Market drink sellers
places.note: Traditional millet and tigernut drinks poured to order in the old market.

places.name: Ten to Ten Restaurant
places.note: Serves kunu and fura da nono alongside its tuwo, if you prefer a table.

landmarks: Kano City Walls and Gates
These centuries-old earthen ramparts once encircled the ancient city and remain punctuated by historic gates like Kofar Mata—an awe-inspiring testament to Kano's medieval trading power.
Kurmi Market
Founded over 500 years ago, this sprawling, labyrinthine market is one of the oldest trading posts in West Africa, brimming with leather, textiles, spices, and traditional crafts.
Gidan Makama Museum
Housed in a former emir's palace of traditional Hausa mud-brick architecture, this museum vividly traces Kano's royal and cultural history through artifacts and art.
Emir's Palace (Gidan Rumfa)
The centuries-old residence of the Emir of Kano is a masterpiece of Hausa architecture and remains the beating heart of the city's royal traditions.
Kofar Mata Dye Pits
Reputedly Africa's oldest surviving dye pits, still in use after 500 years, where indigo-dyed cloth is hand-crafted using centuries-old techniques—an unforgettable photo opportunity.
Kano Central Mosque
A soaring, twin-minaret mosque and one of Nigeria's most important Islamic sites, drawing worshippers and photographers alike with its striking silhouette.
Dala Hill
Believed to be the original settlement site of Kano, this rocky hill offers sweeping views over the old city and is steeped in legend as the city's founding landmark.
Goron Dutse Hill
A rugged hill on Kano's outskirts featuring ancient rock formations and ruins, popular with hikers and history enthusiasts seeking a quieter side of the city.
Tiga Dam
A vast reservoir outside Kano popular for boating, fishing, and birdwatching, offering a scenic escape from the bustling ancient city.
Kano Zoological Garden
One of Nigeria's oldest zoos, this green oasis in the city center is a favorite spot for families and a pleasant break from Kano's historic streets.

train.note: Kano is the northern terminus of the 1,126 km Lagos-Kano narrow-gauge line, rehabilitated in 2013; when it runs the through train takes about 30 hours and costs roughly a quarter of the coach fare, but departures are irregular and often suspended, so check locally before relying on it. The standard-gauge line north from Kano to Maradi in Niger has been under construction for years and carries no passengers. There are no international passenger trains from Nigeria.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches and shared vehicles use the sprawling motor parks around Sabon Gari and the Kano-Zaria road; GIGM (https://gigm.com/) and ABC Transport (https://www.abctransport.com/) sell online, while most other operators take cash at the park. Abuja is 8-9 hours, Kaduna about 3 hours and Lagos 16-20 hours. Cross-border traffic into Niger is handled by minibuses and shared cars via the Katsina/Jibiya or Daura crossings towards Maradi and Zinder rather than by any scheduled international coach, and northern Nigeria's security situation makes overnight road travel unwise.

ferry.note: Kano lies deep in the Sahel roughly 1,000 km from the sea with no navigable river anywhere near it, so there are no ferries or passenger boats.

half.name: Falgore Game Reserve
half.blurb: River rapids, rock outcrops, and the abandoned old settlement of Falgore lie within this protected reserve south of Kano.

full.name: Katsina
full.blurb: A 15th-century minaret modeled on Timbuktu's Sankore Mosque stands in the old walled city that was once a rival trade hub to Kano.
